```{r summary}
# Calculate summaries for reporting
s <- list()

# Demographics
demo <- tbl(duck, "demographics") %>% collect()

# Number of subjects
s$n_players <- nrow(demo) %>% number(big.mark = ",")

# Age interquartile range
s$age_iqr <- quantile(demo$age, probs = c(0.25, 0.75), na.rm = TRUE) %>% 
  paste(collapse = ", ")

# Number of countries
s$n_countries <- length(unique(demo$country[!is.na(demo$country)]))

# Number of different events
s$n_events <- length(unique(events$EventName))

# Number of different variables
s$n_variables <- length(unique(events$Variable))

# Counts of different kinds of events
# Gameplay behaviors
s$events_game <- c(
  "exited_game", 
  "item_purchased", 
  "job_completed", 
  "job_exited", 
  "job_resumed", 
  "job_started",
  "player_logged_in",
  "subtask_completed",
  "task_completed",
  "study_reward_claimed"
)
s$n_events_game <- length(s$events_game)

# Survey response events
s$events_survey <- c(
  "mood_reported", 
  "study_prompt_answered"
)
s$n_events_survey <- length(s$events_survey)

# Status logging events
s$events_status <- c(
  "study_reward_unlocked",
  "update_current_state",
  "game_saved"
  
)
s$n_events_status <- length(s$events_status)

s$obs_per_event <- tibble(
  EventName = c(s$events_game, s$events_survey, s$events_status)
) %>% 
  mutate(
    rows = map_dbl(
      EventName, 
      ~tbl(duck, .x) %>% 
        tally() %>% 
        collect() %>% 
        pull(n)
    )
  )

s$obs_per_event_game <- s$obs_per_event %>% 
  filter(EventName %in% s$events_game) %>% 
  summarise(n = sum(rows)) %>% 
  pull(n) %>% 
  number(big.mark = ",")

s$obs_per_event_survey <- s$obs_per_event %>% 
  filter(EventName %in% s$events_survey) %>% 
  summarise(n = sum(rows)) %>% 
  pull(n) %>% 
  number(big.mark = ",")

s$obs_per_event_status <- s$obs_per_event %>% 
  filter(EventName %in% s$events_status) %>% 
  summarise(n = sum(rows)) %>% 
  pull(n) %>% 
  number(big.mark = ",")
```

---
abstract: |
  The potential impacts that video games might have on players' well-being are under increased scrutiny but poorly understood empirically. Although extensively studied, a level of understanding required to address concerns and advise policy is lacking, at least partly because much of this science has relied on artificial settings and limited self-report data. We describe a large and detailed dataset that addresses these issues by pairing video game play behaviors and events with in-game well-being and motivation reports. `r s$n_players` players (from `r s$n_countries` countries) of the first person PC game PowerWash Simulator volunteered for an experimental version of the game that logged their play across `r s$n_events_game` in-game behaviors and events (e.g. task completion) and `r s$n_variables` variables (e.g. current position), and responses to 6 psychological survey instruments via in-game pop-ups. The data consists of `r s$obs_per_event_game` gameplay events, `r s$obs_per_event_survey` survey item responses, and `r s$obs_per_event_status` additional gameplay status records, and spans `r round(diff(range(dat_survey$Time_utc)))` days. The data and codebook are publicly available with a permissive CC0 license.
---

# Background & Summary

Video games offer billions of players [@newzooNewzooGlobalGames2021], worldwide, opportunities for enjoyment, relaxation, competition, achievement, and socializing [@bowmanSocialVideoGaming2022; @halbrookWhenHowVideo2019]. Although video game play has been studied for decades[@markey2020video], and despite widespread worries and hopes about games' potential consequences[@kollinsNovelDigitalIntervention2020; @mentzoniProblematicVideoGame2011]---and recent policy decisions to address those[@aarsethScholarsOpenDebate2017; @bbcnewsChinaCutsChildren2021; @kardefelt-wintherCriticalAccountDSM52015]---scientists are still uncertain about the psychological effects of play. 
Because many past studies have been limited by inaccurate self-reported play [@kahnWhyWeDistort2014; @parrySystematicReviewMetaanalysis2021], more recent efforts have focused on behavioral telemetry---data that are automatically collected by online game platforms and include player behaviors and in-game events [@johannesTimeSpentPlaying2022; @johannesVideoGamePlay2021; @vuorreLargeScaleStudyChanges2021; @vuorreTimeSpentPlaying2022]. While accurate, that telemetry, or what is made available of it, is typically aggregated and therefore doesn't include potentially critical information about player behaviors and in-game events. As a consequence, while recent studies have been able to measure the quantity of play with great accuracy, the quality of play---what players do and what happens in the game---and its potential effects have remained unknown.

We describe a longitudinal study of video game play behavior, psychological well-being, and human motivations, and the resulting dataset [@vuorrePowerWashSimulatorDataset2022] that includes an unprecedented level of detail about `r s$n_players` players' unaggregated in-game play behaviors and events, in combination with their responses to psychological survey instruments, over `r round(diff(range(dat_survey$Time_utc)))` days of game play. We implemented a modified version of a commercially available game, PowerWash Simulator, that queried participating players' psychological states during play using in-game popups. The combination of detailed play behavior and event data with players' responses to psychological instruments within the game is suitable for both detailed descriptive studies and in-depth statistical modelling of video game play and its relations to players' psychological states. 

# Methods

In this study, we developed a research edition of PowerWash Simulator (PWS)[@futurlabPowerWashSimulatorFuturLab2022], a first-person powerwasher game (see Figure \@ref(fig:fig-pws-play)), and made it available on the same commercial platform (Steam; https://store.steampowered.com/) as the original game. Interested players, recruited via social media, word of mouth, and organic in-game links, downloaded the PWS research edition and gave informed consent to the study and data donation. We first describe the participants and the recruitment process, then the game and the modifications in the research edition, and then the psychological survey instruments that we used.

## Participant recruitment

The main PWS game is available on the Steam platform (at £19.99 on 2022-11-16). The study was first advertised on social media in August of 2022. Both FuturLab and Oxford Internet Institute also hosted websites that advertised the study and instructed potential participants on how to sign up to the study.[@futurlabPowerWashSimulatorResearch2022; @oxfordinternetinstituteOIIResearchersOxford2022] The launch of this study was also noted in news media[@mottPowerWashSimulatorPlayers2022], which may have driven participation.

```{r}
#| label: fig-pws-play
#| include: true
#| out.width: "\\textwidth"
#| fig.env: "figure*"
#| fig-cap: 'Screenshots of PowerWash Simulator gameplay. Top left: Powerwashing a skate park in the Playground level. Top right. Powerwashing a UFO in another level. Bottom left. Looking at the claimed rewards for participation in the study. Bottom right. Providing a Competence response using the in-game pop-up visual analog scale.'
knitr::include_graphics("images/pws.pdf")
```

To participate, players were asked to use Steam to select the publicly available research edition of PWS, and then download it. After their first log-in, but before entering the game menu, participants read our consent form, indicated that they were 18 years or older, and agreed to voluntarily participate in the study. They then optionally answered basic demographic questions and proceeded to play as usual, but with the differences in the game design as discussed below. Eligible participants had to have purchased the game, and we did not pay for participation.

Then, in a second wave of recruitment in January 2023, the main branch of PWS was modified to include a button in the main menu that invited players to participate in the experimental branch. After participants joined the research branch of PWS, they were free to withdraw from the study at any point and return to the main branch of the study, and additionally request to have their data deleted. 

## Participants

```{r}
# Summarise gender
# If player chose multiple categories, we recode it here as "Other"
xd <- demo %>% 
  mutate(gender = if_else(str_detect(gender, ","), "Other", gender)) %>% 
  count(gender) %>% 
  replace_na(list(gender = "Missing")) %>%
  mutate(p = n / sum(n)) %>% 
  arrange(desc(n)) %>% 
  mutate(x = str_glue("{gender}: {n} ({percent(p, .1)})")) %>% 
  pull(x)
```

We defined a participant as anyone who provided informed consent, was over 18 years old, did not request their data to be deleted, and answered at least one survey item. `r number(nrow(demo), big.mark = ',')` players participated, with a median age of `r median(demo$age, na.rm = TRUE)` (10th and 90th percentile: `r quantile(demo$age, c(.1, .9), TRUE)`). The gender breakdown of our sample was as follows: `r paste(xd, collapse = ", ")`.

```{r}
#| label: fig-participation-data
#| include: true
#| fig-height: 3
#| fig.width: 8
#| fig.cap: Summary of each participant's contribution to the study. Both axes are trimmed at 99\%. Filled dark point indicates the bivariate mean.

dat_survey %>%
  arrange(pid, Time_utc) %>%
  select(pid, Time_utc, CurrentSessionLength) %>%
  mutate(
    CurrentSessionLength = as.numeric(CurrentSessionLength),
    session = cumsum(CurrentSessionLength < lag(CurrentSessionLength, default = -1)) + 1,
    n = n(),
    .by = pid
  ) %>% 
  summarise(
    l = max(CurrentSessionLength),
    n = unique(n),
    .by = c(pid, session)
  ) %>%
  summarise(
    l = sum(l),
    n = unique(n),
    .by = pid
  ) %>% 
  filter(l < quantile(l, .99), n < quantile(n, .99)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(l/60, n)) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    "Total hours played",
    expand = expansion(0.02)
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    "Number of survey responses",
    expand = expansion(0.02)
  ) +
  geom_point(
    shape = 1, 
    color = "grey40",
    alpha = .75,
    size = .75,
    position = position_jitter(width = .2)
  ) +
  stat_summary_xy(geom = "point", .fun.y = mean, .fun.x = mean, size = 2.4) +
  theme(aspect.ratio = 1)
ggsave("Figure-2.pdf", width = 3, height = 3)
```

Because participants could withdraw from the research branch at any point, the duration of each player's participation in the study, and the volume of data contributed, could vary. Figure \@ref(fig:fig-participation-data) summarises each participant's contribution to the study.

```{r}
x <- demo %>% 
  count(country) %>% 
  mutate(country = replace_na(country, "Missing data")) %>% 
  arrange(desc(n)) %>% 
  mutate(country = str_glue("{country} (N = {n})"), .keep = "none") %>% 
  pull(country)
# Notice, the number of countries is this -1 because one country is "Missing data".
```

Although the main version of PWS is offered in a number of languages, the experimental version was only offered in English. Nevertheless, participants were located in `r length(x)-1` countries, with varying numbers of players from each country (`r paste0(x, collapse = ', ')`). 

The study procedures were granted ethical approval by Oxford University's Central University Research Ethics Committee (SSH_OII_CIA_21_011). All participants provided informed consent to participate and reported being 18 years or older.

## PowerWash Simulator

In PWS, players control a character whose task is to use a power washer to clean various objects in different environments (Figure \@ref(fig:fig-pws-play); an illustrative video of the actual gameplay on the research edition of PWS is available on YouTube at <https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nIdOILxKsBA> [@futurlabPowerWashSimulatorLaunch2022]). The main game offers a career mode, in which the player progresses through different levels (a garage with a van to be washed, then a backyard with many objects, etc.) by cleaning all the dirty objects in the level. As the players progress, they earn credit which can be used to buy new washing equipment, soaps, and various cosmetic enhancements.

Before the game was released out of early access on Steam, we collaborated with PWS's developer, FuturLab, to implement and make public a modified version of the main game. The academic researchers in our team created the conceptual design of the modifications to the main game, which JB then implemented. That research branch was identical to the main game, except for the following changes: First, it sent detailed game play data such as what happened in the game and when (see Data records, below) to the PlayFab service, from which we continuously exported data to an Amazon Web Services S3 storage bucket for intermediate storage. 

Second, the experimental branch of the game was programmed to surface questions about the players' psychological experiences and states during play using an in-game messaging and response system (Figure \@ref(fig:fig-pws-play)D and Data records, below). Participants could also self-report their mood in the game menu (at most once every 30 minutes). Players' responses to those prompts were sent directly to the academic researchers' Qualtrics database, to which FuturLab members had no access. This ensured the privacy of the participants' survey responses, even from the game developers. 

Participating players received cosmetic items as a form of reward for taking part in the study branch. These were awarded periodically after answering a number of survey items, and were usable in both the research and main versions of PWS. The rewards were not available otherwise in the main version of PWS.

The research edition also featured a "Research Edition" text in the game menu, to remind players that they are in the experimental version, and a button to return to the regular version. The research edition was only available in English, and excluded all downloadable content releases. Finally, although the main game had a multiplayer mode, we disabled that in the research version.

## Survey materials

The research version of PWS was programmed to surface psychological survey items to the player during game, and offered a menu item for self-reporting mood. These questions appeared as in-game pop-ups at most six times per hour of active game play, and with the constraint that they would be at least five minutes apart. Immediately before a survey question appeared, an in-game communication pop-up informed the participant that there would be a survey question soon (seen in the background of Figure \@ref(fig:fig-pws-play)D). While the pop-up was visible, control of the player character was removed and a mouse cursor was made visible, and this was reverted after the participant's response. All responses were optional and players could always click a "Skip" button. There were six different questions, but each pop-up included one item only, chosen at random from the six alternatives. Participants responded to all using a visual analog rating scale (VAS) with 1000 possible values. We show the questions and their associated samples sizes in Table \@ref(tab:tbl-summary-survey).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-summary-survey
#| include: true

dat_survey %>% 
  rename(Item = LastStudyPromptType) %>% 
  mutate(Item = if_else(EventName == "mood_reported", "Wellbeing (menu)", Item)) %>% 
  group_by(Item, pid) %>% 
  mutate(pid_n = n()) %>% 
  group_by(Item) %>% 
  summarise(
    Observations = n(),
    Players = length(unique(pid)),
    `Mdn(o/p)` = as.character(median(pid_n))
  ) %>% 
  mutate(
    across(-Item, ~number(as.numeric(.x), big.mark = ","))
  ) %>% 
  apa_table(
    digits = 0,
    span_text_columns = FALSE, 
    font_size = "small",
    caption = "Counts of survey item responses",
    note = "Mdn(o/p): Median observations per player. 'Wellbeing (menu)' indicates well-being responses that were volunteered through the game menu, instead of provided via the in-game prompts (see main text.)"
  )
```

We queried subjective well-being with *"How are you feeling right now?"* with VAS endpoints *"Very bad"* and *"Very good"* [@killingsworthWanderingMindUnhappy2010]. Although feelings of well-being are often measured with separate positive and negative affect dimensions, our study required the least intrusive item possible to not disrupt play more than was necessary, and we therefore used the simple "happiness" question[@killingsworthWanderingMindUnhappy2010]. Furthermore, such single-item measures have been found to have good validity and are recommended in intensive longitudinal studies [@songExaminingConcurrentPredictive2022]. 

In addition to well-being, we measured motivation and need satisfaction states with widely used items [@ryanMotivationalPullVideo2006]. In order to capture the intrinsically motivating qualities of game play, we queried for "Enjoyment" with *"I was enjoying playing Powerwash Simulator just now."* with VAS endpoints *"Not at all"* to *"As much as possible"* [@johannesVideoGamePlay2021; @johnsonValidationTwoGame2018; @ryanMotivationalPullVideo2006]. 

We were also interested in the broad concept of being focused on playing the game, both in terms of a positively valenced absorption [@csikszentmihalyiFlowPsychologyOptimal2009; @martinBriefApproachesAssessing2008], and a more "meditative" quality of attending rather than allowing one's mind to wander [@mrazekMindfulnessMindwanderingFinding2012; @schoolerMetaawarenessPerceptualDecoupling2011]. We measured this quality of focusing on game play with the prompt *"I was totally focused on playing Powerwash Simulator just now."* and a VAS from *"Not at all"* to *"As much as possible"*.

We also queried for players feelings of autonomy, the degree to which they felt autonomous in their decisions of how to play and what to do in the game, with *"Just now, I was doing the things I really wanted to in Powerwash Simulator"* with VAS endpoints *"Not at all"* and *"As much as possible"*. We queried their feelings of competence with *"Just now, I felt competent playing PowerWash Simulator"*, and feelings of immersion with *"Just now, I felt completely immersed in PowerWash Simulator"*, both with the same VAS as the autonomy item.

```{r}
#| label: fig-response-data
#| include: true
#| fig-height: 5.4
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig.cap: "Survey response volumes over time. A. Counts of daily survey responses and unique players responding to survey items over time. B. Mean counts of survey item observations and unique players over the days of a week. C. Total responses on each day of the week and each hour of the day. All numbers in A-C indicate counts of survey responses only, and not other game play behavior data."
p_timeline <- dat_survey %>% 
  mutate(
    Date = floor_date(Time_utc, "day")
  ) %>% 
  group_by(Date) %>% 
  summarise(Responses = n(), Players = length(unique(pid))) %>% 
  pivot_longer(-Date) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(Date, value)) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    "Count",
    labels = ~number(., big.mark = ",")
  ) +
  scale_x_datetime(
    "Date",
    date_breaks = "1 month", date_labels = "%Y\n%b",
    date_minor_breaks = "week", 
    expand = expansion(0.01)
  ) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap("name", ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(size = rel(0.86)))

p_week <- dat_survey %>% 
  drop_na(Time) %>% 
  mutate(
    Date = floor_date(Time, "day"),
    Weekday = wday(Time, week_start = 1, label = TRUE, abbr = TRUE)
  ) %>% 
  summarise(
    Responses = n(), 
    Players = length(unique(pid)),
    .by = c(Weekday, Date)
  ) %>% 
  summarise(
    `Average responses` = mean(Responses), 
    `Average players` = mean(Players),
    .by = Weekday
  ) %>% 
  pivot_longer(c(`Average responses`, `Average players`)) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(Weekday, value)) +
  scale_colour_viridis_d(direction = -1) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    "Mean count",
    labels = ~number(., big.mark = ",")
  ) +
  scale_x_discrete(
    expand = expansion(0.01)
  ) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7, group = 1) +
  facet_wrap("name", ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  theme(
    axis.title.y = element_blank(), 
    axis.text.x = element_text(size = rel(0.86))
  )

p_hour <- dat_survey %>% 
  drop_na(Time) %>% 
  mutate(
    Hour = hour(Time),
    Weekday = wday(Time, week_start = 1, label = TRUE, abbr = TRUE)
  ) %>% 
  group_by(Weekday, Hour) %>% 
  summarise(
    Observations = n()
  ) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(Hour, Observations, col = Weekday)) +
  scale_colour_viridis_d(direction = -1) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    "Responses",
    labels = ~number(., big.mark = ",")
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = seq(0, 22, by = 2),
    expand = expansion(0.01)
  ) +
  guides(
    color = guide_legend(
      nrow = 1, override.aes = list(linewidth = 1.4))
  ) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

((p_timeline | p_week) + plot_layout(widths = c(6.8, 3.2))) /
  p_hour +
  plot_annotation(tag_level = "A")

ggsave("Figure-3.pdf", width = 8, height = 5.4)
```

The items were surfaced with equal probabilities, but the three latter motivation items were added to the study three weeks after launch. In addition, at every login, there was a 10% probability that the player was asked the well-being item. We summarize the volumes of participants' responses to the survey items, including the in-menu self-reports, in Figure \@ref(fig:fig-response-data).

## Game play data

```{r}
#| label: fig-playday
#| include: true
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig.cap: Figure of one player's game play and survey data for one day. A. Distribution of game play behaviors and events throughout the day. The y-axis indicates different events and behaviors, individual points are observations of those events when they happened (time; x-axis). We jittered the subtask_completed events vertically for visibility. The text labels show example variable values for each event (job_started shows the job name; subtask_completed shows the subtask name). B. Survey responses over time. Lines are exploratory generalized additive model fits.

# Count person-days to choose one with plenty of data for an informative figure
pdays <- dat_survey |> 
  mutate(day = yday(Time)) |> 
  count(pid, day, LastStudyPromptType) |> 
  add_count(pid, day) |> 
  filter(nn == 6) |> 
  summarise(n = sum(n, na.rm = TRUE), .by = c(pid, day)) |> 
  arrange(desc(n))

x <- c(s$events_game, s$events_survey) %>% 
  map(
    ~tbl(duck, .) %>% 
      mutate(day = yday(Time)) |>
      # Pick one person-day here
      right_join(pdays[3, 1:2], copy = TRUE) |>  
      collect()
  ) %>% 
  bind_rows() %>% 
  arrange(pid, Time) |> 
  drop_na(EventName) |> 
  mutate(EventName = fct_inorder(EventName))

date(x$Time) <- as.Date("2022-01-01")
date(x$Time_utc) <- as.Date("2022-01-01")

# Ensure that you are showing just one day and not also previous evening/night
x <- x |> 
  filter(Time > as_datetime("2022-01-01 05:00:00"))

# Highlight a few responses
set.seed(1)
highlights <- x %>% 
  filter(
    EventName %in% c("study_prompt_answered", "subtask_completed", "job_started")
  ) %>% 
  select(
    EventName, Time, LastSubtaskCompleted, 
    CurrentJobName, LastStudyPromptType, response
  ) %>% 
  group_by(EventName, LastStudyPromptType) %>% 
  slice_sample(n = 1) %>% 
  ungroup() %>% 
  mutate(x = factor(1:n())) %>% 
  mutate(LastSubtaskCompleted = str_sub(LastSubtaskCompleted, 23, -1)) %>% 
  mutate(
    label = case_when(
      EventName %in% s$events_survey ~ str_glue("{LastStudyPromptType} ({response})"),
      EventName == "subtask_completed" ~ LastSubtaskCompleted,
      EventName == "job_started" ~ CurrentJobName
    )
  ) %>% 
  replace_na(list(LastStudyPromptType = "Wellbeing"))

p_day_game <- x %>% 
  ggplot(aes(Time, EventName)) +
  scale_y_discrete(position = "right") +
  scale_x_datetime(
    date_breaks = "2 hours", date_labels = "%H:%M"
  ) +
  scale_alpha_manual(values = c(1, .2)) +
  scale_size_manual(values = c(1.75, .75)) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  geom_point(
    position = position_quasirandom(
      groupOnX = FALSE, 
      varwidth = TRUE,
      width = .2
    ),
    aes(
      alpha = EventName == "subtask_completed",
      size = EventName == "subtask_completed"
    ),
    col = "dodgerblue1", size = .75
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = highlights,
    col = "dodgerblue4",
    size = 1
  ) +
  theme(
    axis.title = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "none"
  )


p_day_survey <- x %>% 
  filter(EventName %in% s$events_survey) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(Time, response)) +
  scale_color_brewer(
    "Survey item",
    palette = "Set1"
  ) +
  scale_x_datetime(
    date_breaks = "3 hours", date_labels = "%H:%M"
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    "Response value",
    expand = expansion(0.15)
  ) +
  stat_smooth(
    method = mgcv::gam, 
    formula = y ~ s(x, k = 3, bs = "cr"),
    se = FALSE,
    linewidth = .5,
    col = "dodgerblue4"
  ) +
  geom_point(size = 1, col = "dodgerblue1") +
  facet_wrap(
    "LastStudyPromptType",
    nrow = 2
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

p_day_game <- p_day_game +
  geom_label_repel(
    data = highlights,
    aes(label = label),
    force_pull = 0.0001, fill = alpha("white", 0.5),
    size = 2.8, box.padding = 0.9, 
    min.segment.length = 0,
    segment.color = "dodgerblue4", 
    arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.04, "npc")),
    nudge_y = 1, nudge_x = -3,
    point.padding = 0.33
  )

layout <- "
AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA#
BBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBB
"

(p_day_game / p_day_survey) +
  plot_annotation(tag_level = "A") +
  plot_layout(design = layout)
ggsave("Figure-4.pdf", width = 8, height = 4.2)
```

The research edition of PWS recorded `r s$n_variables` variables describing different facets of the player's status when triggered by one of `r s$n_events_game` in-game play behaviors (e.g. when the player completed a task) or `r s$n_events_status` status updates (e.g. when the game was saved). For example, when the player completed a subtask (e.g. washed a window frame of the mansion; a "subtask_completed" *event*), the game captured and sent the current time (a *variable* with millisecond precision); the name of the subtask; the character's current posture (standing, crouching, or prone); the character's current coordinates in the level; which washer, nozzle, and extension the character was currently using; progression within the level (e.g. 80%); and the current game mode (e.g. career mode or free play). The events and their associated sample sizes are listed in Table \@ref(tab:tbl-summary-events). The spread of these events over a typical day of play are illustrated in Figure \@ref(fig:fig-playday). The events and variables are described in detail in the associated codebook [@vuorrePowerWashSimulatorDataset2022].

```{r}
#| label: tbl-summary-events
#| include: true
c(s$events_game, s$events_status) %>% 
  map(
    ~tbl(duck, .) %>% 
      count(EventName, pid, name = "pid_n") %>% 
      collect()
  ) %>% 
  bind_rows() %>% 
  mutate(EventName = fct_inorder(EventName)) %>% 
  group_by(EventName) %>% 
  summarise(
    Observations = sum(pid_n),
    Players = length(unique(pid)),
    `Mdn(o/p)` = as.character(median(pid_n))
  ) %>% 
  mutate(
    across(-EventName, ~number(as.numeric(.x), 1, big.mark = ","))
  ) %>% 
  apa_table(
    digits = 0,
    font_size = "small",
    span_text_columns = FALSE, 
    placement = "ht",
    midrules = s$n_events_game,
    caption = "Counts of game play events.",
    note = "Mdn(o/p): Median observations per player."
  )
```

However, not all variables were relevant to all events. Therefore, each event only triggered the saving of a subset of variables. In the above example, the "subtask_completed" *event* saved the values of 9 *variables*. The codebook explains which events were paired with which variables. We provide the dataset as a collection of tables, one for each event and only including the variables that were saved during that event. Therefore, for reconstructing more complex timeseries, users can fill relevant values forward or backward in time, wherever appropriate.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-summary-variables
#| eval: false
#| include: true
dbListTables(duck) %>%
  .[-1] %>% 
  map(
    ~tbl(duck, .) %>% 
      select(any_of(c(unique(events$Variable), "Time"))) %>% 
      summarise(across(everything(), ~sum(as.integer(!is.na(.))))) %>% 
      collect()
  ) %>% 
  bind_rows() %>% 
  summarise(across(everything(), ~sum(., na.rm = TRUE))) %>% 
  pivot_longer(
    everything(), 
    names_to = "Variable", 
    values_to = "Count", 
    values_transform = ~number(., big.mark = ",")
  ) %>% 
  apa_table(
    digits = 0,
    font_size = "small",
    span_text_columns = FALSE, 
    caption = "Counts of non-missing Variable values in data"
  )
```

# Data Records

The data and codebook are openly available under a CC-0 license at <https://dx.doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/WPEH6> as a compressed .zip archive of event-specific comma-separated values (.csv) tables [@vuorrePowerWashSimulatorDataset2022]. Those .csv files are exported from a DuckDB database [@muhleisenDuckdbDBIPackage2022], and the repository associated with this manuscript shows examples of loading the tables to a DuckDB database for faster processing. Each row in these tables represents an event that occurred in the game, as listed in Table \@ref(tab:tbl-summary-events), including the survey response events (Table \@ref(tab:tbl-summary-survey)). The columns of those tables are variables of interest, which are further explained in the codebook. In addition, the demographics table includes basic person-level variables, such as the participant's age, gender, country, and total number of survey responses contributed.

# Technical Validation

All data was automatically sent from the game running on the player's device to either the PlayFab service or to the Qualtrics API. Therefore the likelihood of human error in data transport was minimized. Nevertheless, quality considerations remained due to possible technical problems in the internet connection between the player's computer and PlayFab or Qualtrics, and due to improperly configured system clocks on players computers. We make our source code openly available for checking our assumptions regarding these data cleaning steps [@vuorrePowerWashSimulatorDataset2022].

# Usage Notes

The database is already cleaned and ready to be analysed with statistical software. Here, we provide a brief conceptual example on how the data can be used to answer substantive questions. A recent report[@johannesVideoGamePlay2021] found that there is a positive yet exceedingly small relation between time spent playing and well-being, such that people who on average play more tend to report greater well-being. However, that study and others like it have focused on longer time spans (typically two weeks) under which the estimated associations are assumed to operate. The current dataset, with psychological states and play measured practically in the same instance, allows examining associations operating at much shorter time spans.

These data can be readily used to replicate that finding but under different assumptions about time spans in which the associations are assumed to operate. We loaded the "subtask_completed" and "study_prompt_answered" tables from the DuckDB database, aggregated the data to numbers of subtasks completed and mean response values for each individual. We then drew scatterplots and calculated regression slopes to illustrate the associations between average daily subtasks completed, as a proxy for game engagement, and each of the six psychological measures included in the study. The results conceptually replicated [@johannesVideoGamePlay2021]; there was a positive correlation between well-being and game engagement (Figure \@ref(fig:fig-example), "Wellbeing"). The code to conduct these analyses is included in the source repository of this manuscript.

```{r}
#| label: fig-example
#| include: true
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.8
#| fig.cap: An example use of the database showing scatterplots of players' mean item response and average game play engagement (mean subtasks completed per day). Points are individuals, the lines and numbers indicate regression slopes from a censored regression model of the outcome on the log mean number of subtasks completed. Note that the x-axis is on the log scale.

ta <- tbl(duck, "subtask_completed") %>% 
  mutate(day = day(Time)) %>% 
  count(pid, day) %>% 
  summarise(n = mean(n, na.rm = TRUE), .by = pid) %>% 
  collect()
tb <- tbl(duck, "study_prompt_answered") %>% 
  group_by(pid, LastStudyPromptType) %>% 
  summarise(response = mean(response, na.rm = TRUE)) %>% 
  collect()

library(broom)
library(censReg)
x <- left_join(ta, tb) %>% 
  filter(n > 1, response > 1) 
x2 <- x %>% 
  group_by(LastStudyPromptType) %>% 
  drop_na(response) %>% 
  group_modify(
    ~tidy(censReg(response ~ log(n), data = ., left = 0, right = 1000))
  ) %>% 
  ungroup() %>% 
  filter(term == "log(n)") %>% 
  mutate(
    r = str_glue(
      "r = {number(estimate, .01)} (SE = {number(std.error, .01)}) "
      )
    )
x %>% 
  drop_na(LastStudyPromptType) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(n, response)) +
  scale_color_viridis_c(aesthetics = c("color", "fill")) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    "Mean item response",
    breaks = extended_breaks()
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    "Mean number of subtasks completed per day",
    breaks = breaks_log(),
    trans = "log"
  ) +
  geom_point(
    alpha = .33,
    size = .33,
    shape = 1,
    col = "dodgerblue1"
  ) +
  geom_text(
    data = x2,
    aes(label = r, x = Inf, y = -Inf), 
    size = 3,
    vjust = -0.8, hjust = 1
  ) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  facet_wrap("LastStudyPromptType") +
  theme(
    aspect.ratio = 1,
    plot.margin = unit(rep(14, 4), "pt")
    )
ggsave("Figure-5.pdf", width = 8, height = 4.2)
```

# Code Availability

The data used to clean the raw data is openly available at <https://dx.doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/WPEH6> [@vuorrePowerWashSimulatorDataset2022]. We processed the raw JSON files created by the game using jq and PostgreSQL. We then used R [@rcoreteamLanguageEnvironmentStatistical2023] to post-process those files, including replacing the (already hashed) player IDs with new IDs to prevent reidentification of players by FuturLab Ltd.
